analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans to cover reconstructive surgery for children with birth defects, deformities, or injuries.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the Senate health committee and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the laws governing employer health plans, private insurance, and the tax code to require coverage of a minor child's congenital or developmental deformity, disease, or injury. It defined 'treatment' to include reconstructive surgery on abnormal body structures caused by birth defects, trauma, infection, tumors, or disease — even procedures that improve appearance rather than function — while excluding purely cosmetic surgery. It died in committee without ever coming up for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with children born with or who develop deformities — such as cleft lip and palate, craniofacial differences, or disfigurement from injury, infection, or tumors — would gain required insurance coverage for diagnosis and reconstructive treatment, including surgery that improves appearance rather than body function, through age 22. Families would no longer have to pay out of pocket for procedures insurers can currently deny as cosmetic.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families of children needing reconstructive surgery

how_it_helps.text: It requires any group health plan or insurer that covers surgical benefits to cover diagnosis and treatment of a child's congenital or developmental deformity, disease, or injury — including reconstructive procedures that improve appearance but not function, and follow-up and secondary treatments.

Coverage must include any surgical treatment the treating physician deems medically necessary to approximate a normal appearance, closing the common coverage gap where plans deny procedures as 'cosmetic'.
It excludes purely cosmetic surgery on normal body structures, limiting the mandate to genuinely reconstructive care.

analysis.who_pays: Employers and health insurers offering plans with surgical benefits would bear the added cost of covering children's reconstructive care, likely passed on in premiums to enrollees and plan sponsors generally.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers, employers, and premium payers

drawbacks.text: The mandate raises plan costs: every plan or insurer covering surgical benefits must pay for diagnosis and treatment of children's deformities from birth through age 22, which would flow into higher premiums for employers and enrollees.

The bill defers to the treating physician's judgment that a procedure is medically necessary to 'approximate a normal appearance', limited only by pre-authorization rules the plan itself sets, which critics of broad medical-necessity mandates could argue invites expansive interpretation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — coverage for children's reconstructive surgery, sparing families crushing out-of-pocket bills for treatment that is not optional — is real and the costs, higher premiums spread across all insured people, are modest and diffuse. The bill was narrow and reasonably written, with a pre-authorization safeguard and a cosmetic-surgery exclusion. Its main weakness is procedural: it sat in committee with no markup, no hearing, and no vote, so no cost-benefit weighing ever happened on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate health committee on the day it was introduced and never came out, so it died quietly when the 111th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 11, 2009 and read twice, then referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions — its last recorded action.
Eight senators cosponsored it, split between one Republican and seven Democrats, but it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 with the bill still in committee, so it died without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurers and employers that would have had to pay for children's reconstructive care benefit from the bill's death; families of children with congenital deformities continue to bear those costs themselves.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers who avoided the mandate

for.name: Sen. Mary Landrieu
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its sponsorship.

for.name: Sens. Thad Cochran, Arlen Specter, and Evan Bayh
for.what_they_did: Joined the introduction as original cosponsors, giving the bill bipartisan backing.

for.name: Senate HELP Committee
for.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action on it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had support from members of both parties — 7 of 58 Senate Democrats and 1 of 40 Senate Republicans cosponsored — but opposition is not visible in the record; the bill simply died in committee without a vote.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer health plans
industries.note: The bill would have required plans and insurers covering surgical benefits to also cover children's reconstructive care, adding claims they currently can deny as 'cosmetic'. For ordinary families this means coverage for a child's cleft lip, birth defect repair, or injury reconstruction without paying out of pocket.

A federal coverage mandate would expand the pool of covered patients for reconstructive surgery on children, including procedures the bill explicitly covers even when they do not affect body function.
